newsitem.title: USA: Small-town prosecutor gears up for Kevorkian trial.
newsitem.headline: Small-town prosecutor gears up for Kevorkian trial.

text.p: Ray Voet will try next week to succeed where two other Michigan prosecutors have failed on three occasions: putting "Dr. Death" behind bars.

Jury selection for the fourth trial of Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the world's best-known crusader for assisted suicide, was scheduled to begin Tuesday in this conservative, well-kept town set amid rolling farm land in west-central Michigan.

Kevorkian, who has admitted attending 45 deaths since 1990, was charged with four felonies including violating the state's unwritten "common law" banning physician-assisted suicide for his role in the Aug. 30 death of Loretta Peabody, who suffered from multiple sclerosis. He was also charged with practicing medicine without a license.

The odd-couple duo of Kevorkian, the fiery 69-year-old retired pathologist dubbed "Dr. Death" by the media, and Geoffrey Fieger, his swaggering, caustic lawyer, prevailed every time they faced prosecutors in the Detroit area.

But this time the trial will be in different, and perhaps more hostile, territory. Ionia is Ray Voet's home turf. He grew up in the mostly Republican, mostly Catholic town of 7,000, which is home to five state prisons that employ 2,200.
Sitting in his office in Ionia County's 112-year-old courthouse this week, Voet (pronounced Vote) told Reuters that he did not seek out the area's biggest case in 50 years.

"I never asked for this. I'm not a publicity seeker," he said. "The only thing that matters to me when this is all said and done is if I still have a family and a life in this town. That sounds corny, but it's true."

Voet, whose budget was $298,000 last year, was an unlikely candidate to take on the multimillion dollar legal machine that has gotten Kevorkian off three times before. With his buzz-cut hair, the 35-year-old father of three looks the part of the third-generation law enforcement official that he is.
He is unpretentious, soft-spoken and boyish. Light-coloured hair on the carpet in his office showed that the family's yellow Labrador retriever, Maize, is a frequent visitor.
Colleagues gave Voet points for being well-prepared, sensitive and polite. But they said he does not dazzle juries with a riveting courtroom presence.

A big fan of Bruce Springsteen, Voet said he appreciates the real people with real problems that the New Jersey-born rock star sings about. Voet often felt for sorry for criminals he prosecuted, but that does not change what he regards as Kevorkian's flagrant disregard for the law.
"I may have personal feelings about abortion, but Roe v. Wade is the law," he said. "We're not a nation of anarchy, and Kevorkian is behaving as an anarchist."

Indeed, Kevorkian's lawyers were worried enough that he might misbehave in court that they asked Ionia Circuit Court Judge Charles Miel to excuse him from attending the trial. Miel, who took office in January, was considering the request.
Kevorkian entered the courthouse at his last trial wearing a Thomas Jefferson wig and tricorner hat to mock the "Old English" common law used to prosecute him.

David Bulling, the Ionia police detective investigating the case, believes Ionia stands the best chance of convicting Kevorkian of any county in Michigan -- as long as jurors are not swayed by the emotional aspects of the issue.

"I think people in Ionia County certainly follow the law better than people in other areas because they have more of a sense of what the criminal justice system is all about and they have respect for the system," Bulling said.
